text: Cassini had very little fuel left, so rather than leave it drifting, mission control deliberately aimed it into Saturn’s upper atmosphere. The worry was forward contamination. The spacecraft had left Earth and flown past Jupiter, so it could carry microscopic hitchhikers. If it had wandered into Enceladus’s orbit and hit that moon, those organisms might reach its subsurface ocean, which is one of the best places to look for life. Hitting Saturn removed that chance and also gave a final close look at the rings before burnup. Honestly, it was less dramatic than a full orbit insertion, but enough to make the end useful.

Honestly, your standing leg is carrying way more than you think. When you're riding, that leg is doing the bracing, the fine adjustments, and basically all the stabilization. If it hurts, it's usually because the muscles around the hip and thigh are getting hammered. The adductors especially are working overtime trying to keep you from falling. If your stance is off or you're leaning too hard onto that side, the strain multiplies fast. I've seen plenty of riders blame the board or the wheels when the real problem is their leg is just tired from doing too much work. You could also be tightening up your hip flexors and getting that dull ache at the groin or upper thigh. The fix is not to stop riding entirely, but to loosen up and check your stance. You might be favoring one side and overloading that leg. A few minutes of gentle hip and thigh stretching before you ride helps, and keeping your knees bent softens the impact. If the pain sticks around, back off a bit and let it rest for a day or two, but if it becomes sharp or keeps coming back after rest, that's worth having someone look at it. It's not just a bad board. Your leg is telling you it's been doing extra work you haven't noticed.

That is mostly a question of ancestry rather than where someone was born. When people say Afro-American, they usually mean American Black people whose family history traces back to Africa, most often through West and Central African ancestors brought over during the transatlantic slave trade. So the label points to roots, not current residence. A lot of Black Americans have been in the country for many generations, and they are not expected to have personally grown up in Africa. The phrase can sound odd if you think it means someone actually comes from Africa today, but historically it was used to connect Black Americans to their African heritage. It is also worth noting that not every Black American can name a specific African country, and many have mixed ancestry, but the broad cultural and historical link is what makes the term meaningful. Some use it proudly, and some do not care for the term, but the underlying idea is the same: African roots in an American context. That distinction is the whole point.

Honestly, in a country like Syria the answer is messier than one warehouse. Some arms come from the state, local workshops, captured gear, and smuggling routes, especially when the center doesn't control everything. You also get black market flow from neighbors and older stock resurfacing. And if a faction gets backed by money or allies, the flow doesn't slow down much. The reason they still get them is that guns have become almost normal. When you have several armed actors and no single strong state, a rifle is still a faster fix than waiting for politics to sort itself out. So demand keeps the supply moving.

Hi there,
I'd suspect it's mostly the combination of a lot of standing and carrying plus the stress of keeping up on a long shopping trip. That kind of day can load your back, legs, and shoulders, and if you're not drinking enough water or eating properly, you can get a dull, heavy ache that feels less like a normal headache and more like everything is tense and tired. It's not just in your head. I'd try better shoes, taking real breaks, and making sure you're not gripping your arms while carrying bags, and that adds up fast.

Best,
Me

Hi Sam,

I wouldn't worry about it. The silk repetition is probably just priming your brain, making you think in a fixed way. Then "what do cows drink" is a tricky question because milk is the thing people most strongly associate with cows. You probably slipped into the common association, not into some medical explanation. It's exactly the kind of thing where your brain goes with the obvious link rather than the factual answer. Water is what cows actually drink, so your instinct was understandable. If he was trying to catch you off guard, that was the trick. It's not about what you said that matters, just that your brain took the most natural route.

Best,
Alex

Inbreeding doesn't work by one magic gene for intelligence. Parents who are related share more of the same mutations, so a child gets two copies of the same bad variant much more often. Many of these variants are recessive, meaning one copy is usually harmless, but two copies can mess with brain development, hormone signaling, or basic cell repair. That raises the chance of inbreeding depression, which is a broad drop in health and cognitive performance, not just IQ. IQ is also polygenic, with hundreds of small effects, so related families tend to cluster toward lower scores when rare harmful alleles get exposed. Most related children are still fine, yet the group average drops because the same hidden mutations surface more often. The science is basically probability: the closer the parents, the higher the chance both carry the same mutation, and the more visible the problems become.

A lot of what we call well-known brands only became possible after industrialization. Before the industrial era, most businesses were local workshops or family firms, serving nearby customers. Their scale was small, and survival depended on craft and local reputation, so they rarely built the mass-production and distribution networks needed for national or global recognition. Industrialization changed that by enabling standardized products, larger factories, and modern marketing and communication. Many older firms also did not survive, or left few clear records. So the absence of famous pre-industrial brands reflects how industrialization made long-lived, wide-reaching companies much more likely.

Last year, while shopping for a car, I made the mistake of thinking the lowest advertised rate meant the cheapest loan. The dealership offered 5.9% for a 60-month term, while my local bank quoted 6.4% for 72 months. On paper, the dealer looked better. In reality, my bank loan cost less. That experience pushed me to a firm position: a dealership's lower interest rate does not make the dealer the cheaper choice, because the dealer's rate is usually only part of the total cost.

The dealer's low rate came with a bundle I didn't need. There was a $1,200 documentation fee, a $350 dealer preparation charge, and a $500 service plan that was nearly mandatory if I wanted the advertised price. The bank, on the other hand, gave me a straightforward loan with only a small origination fee and no forced add-ons. When I added up the dealer fees, the 5.9% rate stopped looking attractive. The longer bank term also spread payments over more months, and I could choose my own maintenance and insurance.

There is a subtle trick in dealership financing. The advertised rate may be subsidized, but it often applies only to selected vehicles or selected terms. If you want a different car or a longer repayment period, the rate can jump. Banks may not have the flashiest number, but they let you compare the real total. I could even pay down principal at the bank to reduce the balance, something the dealer package didn't easily allow. So the bank being cheaper isn't because its interest rate is lower. It's because the bank's total cash outlay, after fees and term length, was lower. If you only compare APRs, you can walk into a dealership, get the low-rate offer, and still pay more overall. It is also worth remembering that a lower dealer rate can be conditional. If you change the car, length, or down payment, the discount may vanish, while the bank's rate stays steady. I still think a bank can be cheaper even when its APR is higher. The math is about total dollars, not a percentage.

My rule now is simple: ignore the headline rate and calculate total payments, fees, and interest over the full loan. That is where the real cost lives. A bank may quote a slightly higher percentage, yet be cheaper because it avoids dealer markups and bundled products. The dealership's lower rate is real, but it is not the whole story. That is the simple lesson I learned the expensive way.

I think the patchwork of marijuana laws in the US is about as useful as a map drawn by someone who only owns half the pen. Some states let you grow your own, some sell it in shops, and some still arrest people for small amounts. In California, you can buy a joint at a dispensary, while in places like Texas the rules are much stricter. It’s weird how much it changes depending on the border you cross. I’m for letting states keep experimenting, but federal law still calls it illegal, which makes doing business or even traveling a headache. What I miss is clarity. A person can be legal in one state and technically illegal at the federal level, and nobody really explains that to beginners. I don’t want every state to have the same rules. I want the federal government to stop treating each state’s choice like a crime scene.

My favorite way to think about it is that the body isn't making electricity from nothing. The heart, nerves, and muscles use ion gradients already set up by sodium-potassium pumps that burn ATP. When a neuron fires, the membrane briefly lets sodium rush in, flipping the cell's voltage and sending a signal down the axon. That tiny voltage difference, a fraction of a volt, is enough to make a muscle fiber twitch. The real magic isn't sparks; it's careful ion bookkeeping, and that bookkeeping is what keeps you alive. I keep coming back to that, and it still helps me.

I used to think a headache meant my brain was swelling, but the pain isn't coming from the brain tissue itself. My own pattern is pretty clear: after long screen time, a skipped meal, or too little sleep, I feel pressure behind the eyes first, then a dull throbbing at the temples. That's usually the scalp, the membranes around the brain, and the nerves in the head getting irritated. The trigeminal nerve, which runs through the face and skull, is the main messenger here. When it's sensitized, chemicals released in the area make the pain worse. For me, the fix is boring: water, food, rest, and getting away from the screen. It's not a brain injury, just a signal that the basics got ignored. Sometimes the trigger is dehydration, but sleep and food hit me hardest.

I can’t tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We showed up at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday. We picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show at the same hotel and thought it would be easy. We put our names on their digital waitlist, which was useless, and they told us to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but stood around until 8:40 p.m. before anyone mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. It was two of us, and they offered zero help. If your wait runs that far past payment, tell people up front so our night isn't wasted. Total mess. Zero stars if that were an option.

About two years ago I ordered two shirts for my dad over the phone from Rockmount Ranch Wear. They never showed up. The sales rep had written down the address wrong; her handwritten 7 looked like a 1 to whoever processed it. It should have gone to 5407, but it went to 5401. The people at 5401 took it into their local UPS store to send it back. The package then vanished. We didn’t find out for several weeks. In the middle of arguing with the company, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the first two. At that point the owner stepped in. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund unless the shirts came back. He said we were partly to blame for not being friendly enough to the folks at 5401, just four doors away. We ended up disputing the original charge with our credit-card company, and we eventually got a credit.
